The Chapter of the Cat and Rat

p.n: The King Asks about Escaping Enemies

body.p:
“I have heard this parable,” said King Dabīshalm to the Philosopher Baydabā. “Present to me now a parable about a man
whose enemies were many and surrounded him on every side, so that he was on their account on the brink of perishing; from whom he, therefore, sought safety
and a way out by partnering with one of the enemies, reconciling with him; who was thus saved from his fear and felt secure;
and who then kept his promise to the one enemy whom he had reconciled
with.”

p.n: The Philosopher Responds that Emotions Change

body.p:
The Philosopher said: “Amity and enmity do not sustain the same state forever: amity might
become enmity and enmity might transform into amity. This entails circumstances, causes, and experiences;

and so a man of reason creates for whatever happens a new judgment: for that which comes from the enemy, he uses boldness;
and for that which comes from friends, he fosters intimacy.

p.n: Enmity Must Not Stop One from Requesting Help

body.p:
Enmity does not hinder a man of reason from <> someone who had shown him hostility to seek his aid,
if he desires him to avert a scary matter or attract a desired thing;
for he who acts diligently with regards to that will attain his need.

p.n: The Parable of the Cat and Rat Is Invoked

body.p:
An example of this is the parable of the cat and the rat,
when they fell into trouble, yet were both saved, upon reconciling
with one another, from dire difficulty.”

p.n: The King Requests the Full Parable

body.p: “And how was that?” said the King.
